Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Federal agents stand outside the Delaney Hall immigration detention facility in Newark, New Jersey in May. Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) Alarm over $20m plan to supply ICE officers with electric-shock gloves Civil liberties groups decry plan to use gloves linked to death of Kentucky man allegedly shocked 27 times in county jail Sara Braun Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 07.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Plans to supply Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers with special gloves that can deliver electric shocks have alarmed experts and drawn scrutiny amid some high-profile lawsuits over their use in local correctional facilities. In one extreme case, a 43-year-old man died after allegedly being shocked 40 times by officers with a combination of the gloves and a Taser in a county jail in Kentucky, and the man’s widow is suing authorities . Earlier this month, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, published plans to spend up to $20m (£15m) to outfit ICE officers by March of next year with the controversial gloves, which are also used in various police departments and some schools. Civil rights advocates protest that the federal agency’s use of force during Donald Trump’s immigration crackdowns already lacks proper oversight . ICE “is putting these [gloves] in the hands of an agency that has dropped its hiring standards, its training, its background requirements in its hiring spree ”, Sarah Mehta, deputy director of government affairs in the equality division of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), said. “We’re already seeing the consequences of that in lawless and violent enforcement actions in our streets,” she told the Guardian. “What’s really terrifying is use of them on the streets, potentially to terrify people, to create a chilling effect. But what’s also scary is what [their] uses will be where we can’t see them. We don’t know how they’re going to be used in places like Fort Bliss ,”she added, referring to the largest migrant detention facility in the US, where allegations of abuse are legion. The government denies claims of any inhumane conditions. Mehta further said of the gloves: “There are no circumstances where we think their use is appropriate.” The device carries the brand name G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and is manufactured by Compliant Technologies , a company owned by military veterans and based in Lexington, Kentucky. The glove is known as a conductive distraction and de-escalation deviceand can only be sold to certain verified entities, such as law enforcement, corrections, security, military, and emergency medical services (EMS) personnel, and requires training. It works by delivering an electric shock when the user pushes a button on the glove and touches or grips bare skin. In one demonstration video, a man gives a brief, light touch for approximately one second to the lower back of a prone volunteer, who jerks his body and cries out: “Ow, fuck”. Shock gloves demo Compliant Technologies has posted multiple video demonstrations on its Instagram page. In one video from November 2025, a woman wearing the glove grips firmly on the exposed forearm of a volunteer man for about two seconds. The man buckles to the ground, shouting expletives and says “Let me go!” “I’m going to comply any time,” the man says from the ground in a half-humorous tone to the team running the demonstration. Jeff Niklaus, founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, can be seen laughing in the video as the man fell to the ground. “Say that louder,” he says. The man, seemingly a prospective customer, says: “Yeah, we need that [product].” Compliant Technologies did not respond to a series of questions and requests for comment from the Guardian. A DHS spokesperson sent this statement in response to questions: “ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country. “Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards.” The minimum voltage for the CT-G5 model is 324 volts, and the maximum is 380 volts. A Taser, by contrast, can typically fire prongs from a distance to incapacitate someone with 1,200 to 1,500 volts. The glove user manual instructs wearers to avoid using the product on elderly people, small children, pregnant women and disabled people. The gloves have been deployed to a limited extent in law enforcement, healthcare, and even some educational environments across the country. An estimated 50 police departments across 20 states are using the technology, according to an NPR analysis. In May 2025, the Omaha police department purchased 40 pairs of gloves to be used in public schools for just under $66,000, according to city documents . The department confirmed in a statement that 29 of its 34 school resource officers (SROs) – typically police providing security full time in schools – have trained in use of the gloves and work in public middle and high schools. A representative from the Omaha police department shared with the Guardian the report from an incident where the G.L.O.V.E. was used. The report says a female SRO used the shock glove on a male middle school student based on his “highly aggressive and assaultive behavior”. The officer placed the glove on the student’s forearm twice, once for one second, and then again for two to three seconds, which, the report continued, caused the student to drop to the floor, face down. According to the report, the SRO asked if the student needed medical assistance after being shocked, and he said no. Last week, Omaha police acceded to a request from the school superintendent to discontinue the gloves in Omaha, Nebraska’s largest public school district, NBC reported . In a very different example, Joshua Elswick, formerly detained at the Bullitt county jail in Shepherdsville, near Louisville, Kentucky, sued Lt Ryan Derrough alleging excessive force, after Derrough, a guard, used the gloves on Elswick during pre-trial detention. Elswick, who has paranoid schizophrenia and other serious mental illnesses, according to the lawsuit , was arrested and booked into jail in September 2022 after a domestic dispute involving methamphetamine use. Derrough and another deputy attempted to remove Elswick’s handcuffs and leg shackles before formally taking him into custody, but Elswick was paranoid that the officers were going to kill him and he resisted, whereupon Derrough shocked Elswick with the gloves, according to the lawsuit. The incident can be seen in surveillance footage featured in a report on the case from Kentucky TV station WDRB. The footage shows a tense scene, with the guard wearing bright yellow gloves and using them on Elswick, who is struggling against three guards, and yells out. The Kentucky federal court dismissed Elswick’s lawsuit in June 2025, finding that Derrough’s use of force was warranted, a decision upheld by an appeals court in January. A representative for APB Consulting Solutions, a dealer and training partner for Compliant Technologies’ product, told WDRB in 2022 that agencies undergo a lot of training and that used properly the gloves can prevent further injury – while it is recommended not to apply them for more than 15 seconds. Sara Collins, a lawyer representing Elswick, declined to comment on the specific civil case, but told the Guardian: “With proper training and use, effective, less-lethal force options are much-needed resources in law enforcement. Shock gloves, however, are not a new tool.” “I am troubled by the fact that the overwhelming majority of law enforcement agencies across the country do not use them,” she added, noting that relatively few departments out of 18,000 across the US have bought the gloves. “Feasibility, practicality, training, risk of error, and intent are among my many concerns about their implementation by ICE,” Collins said. Meanwhile, Johnathan Mansfield, who was arrested on a public intoxication charge in 2024, suffered a cardiac arrest two weeks after he was allegedly shocked 27 times with the gloves and 13 times by a Taser at Madison county detention center in Richmond, Kentucky, according to the lawsuit filed by Mansfield’s family against the authorities, claiming wrongful death. The complaint alleges : “An internal investigation by the Madison County Detention Center found that ‘ ... Mr Manfield [sic] suffered a cardiac arrest following the series of Taser and G.L.O.V.E. exposures.’” The internal investigation, as cited in the lawsuit, stated that “four distinct use of force incidents were recorded… resulting in a total of 13 taser exposures – comprising both probes and drive-stun applications – lasting between 23 to 28 seconds. Additionally, there were 27 exposures using the G.L.O.V.E.” One of the shock glove exposures lasted for 45 seconds and another for 99 seconds, the document alleges. The suit, filed in a Madison county, Kentucky circuit court, is still pending. https://www.politico.eu/article/nato-rea.text: NATO is ready to respond to a potential Russian escalation on Europe’s eastern flank, the alliance's top general Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said Saturday, amid growing warnings of a possible staged attack by Moscow. “The alliance is ready, the structure is ready, the soldiers … the weapons are ready,” Dragone told reporters during a regular meeting of the alliance’s 32 top generals in Copenhagen, adding that NATO was continuing its work in “increasing” these forces “in number … and also in sophistication.” The remarks follow growing warnings by European leaders about a possible Russian escalation in Europe . On Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Moscow could send drones or missiles into a frontline NATO country in “the next few months” in a staged provocation to test the alliance — a risk that was later echoed by France and the Netherlands. Advertisement Advertisement Europe has grappled with a growing number of airspace violations and sabotage attempts in recent weeks, as tensions with Russia continue to rise over its full-scale war in Ukraine. In August, U.S. intelligence reports warned that Moscow was planning a limited assault on a NATO country in the coming years. Dragone, the chair of NATO’s military committee, said the alliance’s generals on Saturday did not discuss the latest warnings but argued NATO had “4,000 pages” of military plans ready for protecting its eastern flank, starting from scenarios involving a “minimal crisis or interference [on] our soil.” NATO allies agreed on three operational regional defense plans in 2023 following Moscow's all-out invasion of Ukraine. Allies are “ready in case of an escalation,” Dragone said. “In case of an attack, we know how to do it.” “Russia’s reckless behaviour over the last weeks and months … continues to test allied resolve” and “aims to undermine trust and weaken our unity,” Dragone said, adding: “I want to be clear — these attempts are not dividing us. They are sharpening our tools, making us much more united and determined.”

https://thecolu.mn/5300/maja-t-faces-app.text: Politics September 22, 2026 Maja T. Faces Appeal Trial as Prosecution Seeks Longer Prison Sentence Seven months after Maja T.’s eight-year prison sentence was handed down, Budapest’s appeal proceedings have begun. The non-binary individual from Jena, associated with the left-wing scene, was convicted in February at first instance of allegedly serious bodily harm committed against suspected far-right extremists in Hungary (this was reported by TheColu.mn). The prosecution is now seeking a harsher penalty, while the defense calls for acquittal. The alleged acts are tied to violent actions by a German Antifa group, for members of which verdicts have already been issued in Germany. With the final appellate decision for Maja T. anticipated on September 30, observers will be watching closely. Prosecutor Seeks Stricter Sentence The public prosecutor requested an increase of Maja T.’s prison term to more than 13 years; the legal range for the charged offenses spans from two to 24 years. The precise sentence sought was not named, which, according to experts, aligns with common practice in Hungary. In addition, the prosecution urged a tougher prison regime: rather than serving the term in a standard penitentiary, Maja T. should be confined in a so-called “zuchthaus.” In Hungary, a zuchthaus means reduced freedom of movement within the facility and stricter conditions for early release. The prosecutor objected that the court in the first instance did not recognize that the suspect may have consciously accepted the potential for life-threatening injuries to the victims. The charges and the requested penalties reflect a broader concern about violence linked to a German Antifa group, whose members have faced legal actions in both Hungary and Germany. The courtroom argument underscored the seriousness with which Budapest authorities treat assaults believed to be connected to political extremism on Hungarian soil. Defense Questions the Evidence and Seeks Acquittal The defense argued that Maja T.’s identification on street surveillance footage from the scene is not definitively conclusive. Further, defense counsel contended that there is no proof that the Budapest-based Antifa circle linked to the case constitutes a criminal association as defined by criminal law. A medical expert who testified did not provide unequivocal evidence that the victims were attacked with weapons such as clubs. The defense also raised a procedural rights issue, arguing that not all relevant materials were made available to the defendant in a German translation, potentially impairing the right to a fair trial. Maja T. was arrested in December 2023 in Berlin and was extradited from Germany to Hungary in June 2024. The Federal Constitutional Court later determined that the extradition in this form was unlawful, because the chamber court that had ordered it had not sufficiently scrutinized the detention conditions in Hungary. T. has repeatedly described mistreatment in Hungary, attributing it to prejudice against her gender identity. Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Register for FREE Webinar Register for FREE Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato member within the coming months, Denmark's intelligence service has warned, raising fresh concerns about Moscow's intentions towards the military alliance. According to the Financial Times, the Danish Defence Intelligence Service said there was a “low but growing risk” that Russia could move a small number of troops, potentially without insignia, into a neighbouring Nato country or use long-range weapons against infrastructure supporting Ukraine. The warning represents one of the clearest assessments yet from a western intelligence service about the possibility of a limited Russian military operation against a Nato member. Thomas Ahrenkiel, head of the Danish intelligence service, said such an operation could involve Russian forces entering a limited area inside a Nato country bordering Russia. One possible justification, he said, could be the claimed protection of Russian minorities. The broader objective could be to create divisions within the alliance. Ukraine criticises South Korea over 176,000 tonnes of fuel shipped to Russia Hybrid attacks raise concern The warning comes amid a series of incidents across Europe that governments have linked to Russian hybrid warfare and sabotage. These include a foiled drone attack involving Leipzig airport in Germany and an incident in which a Russian ship reportedly fired flares at a Danish helicopter over the Baltic Sea. Poland also said Russia was probably behind an arson attack on a Starlink ground station. The facility was intended to support internet services used by Ukraine. Polish digital minister Krzysztof Gawkowski described such incidents as part of hybrid and sabotage warfare, saying signs pointed towards Russian involvement. Danish intelligence warned that Moscow could intensify such operations, with attacks potentially causing greater disruption and casualties. It highlighted the possibility of destructive cyberattacks capable of disrupting essential societal functions, alongside sabotage operations carrying a high risk of casualties. Russia faces pressure The Danish assessment also said Russia was under greater pressure than at any point since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. At the same time, the intelligence service said there was no prospect of Moscow achieving a major breakthrough in Ukraine during the next six months. Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus said Russia's difficulties were driving its focus towards countries supporting Ukraine. He argued that attacks against European infrastructure demonstrated the pressure Moscow was facing. Full-scale war remains unlikely Despite the warning, Danish intelligence said a full-scale Russian invasion of a Nato country remained highly unlikely in the immediate future. Such an operation would require a major military build-up lasting about six months, according to the assessment. However, the intelligence service said the possibility could not be completely ruled out. It estimated that Russia would need around six months to wage a local war against a neighbouring Nato country, two years to pose a credible threat of a regional war and five years to launch a large-scale war in Europe. Western intelligence services have previously warned that Moscow could potentially turn its attention towards Nato within three to five years, particularly if the war in Ukraine ends. But Denmark's latest assessment suggests Russia could escalate its confrontation with the West sooner through hybrid attacks or a limited military operation, even while fighting in Ukraine continues.
